faq.q: Is spider silk stronger than steel?
faq.a: Weight for weight, dragline silk is about as strong as high-grade steel, and it is far tougher, meaning it absorbs much more energy before snapping. A thread of steel the same thickness would be stronger but much heavier.
asks: Is spider silk really stronger than steel?
What does tough mean for a material?

faq.q: Why is spider silk so tough?
faq.a: Silk mixes hard protein crystals, which give strength, with springy tangled protein chains, which let it stretch. Being both strong and stretchy lets it soak up the energy of a flying insect without breaking.
asks: How does a web stop a fast insect?
Why doesn't a web break when a bug hits it?

faq.q: Which spider makes the toughest silk?
faq.a: Darwin's bark spider from Madagascar makes the toughest biological material known, roughly twice as tough as other spider silks. Its webs stretch across rivers, held by lines up to 25 metres long.
asks: What is the toughest natural material?

faq.a: Spiders cannot be farmed like silkworms because they eat each other. Scientists put silk genes into bacteria, yeast and even goats to make silk protein, but spinning it as well as a spider does is still hard.
asks: Why don't we farm spiders for silk?
Can we make artificial spider silk?

faq.q: How much can spider silk stretch?
faq.a: Dragline silk can stretch by about 30 percent before breaking, and the sticky capture spiral can stretch to two or three times its length.
asks: How far does a spider web stretch?

facts: Spider dragline silk has a toughness of about 160 megajoules per cubic metre, about three times Kevlar and over 20 times high-tensile steel (Gosline and others, 1999).
Silk from Darwin's bark spider averages about 350 megajoules per cubic metre, the toughest biological material measured (Agnarsson and others, 2010).
